title: Ang 664–690: the Gurus in Dhanasri
hookLine: whatever you ask of your Master, on ang 681
tomorrow: if what you're after is close, why go searching the forest?

lines: THE CART YOU NEVER CHECK OUT.
cards: Birthday lists, wish lists, the cart full of things you'll never check out. Asking comes easily when the asking is for stuff. Yesterday's question was harder: if you could ask for anything, what would it be?
On ang 681, Guru Arjan says something that sounds like a blank check. Whatever I ask of my Master, he gives me.

teach.b: These pages hold the Gurus' hymns in Dhanasri, in order: Guru Amar Das, Guru Ram Das, then Guru Arjan.
And here's his line, in paraphrase: whatever I ask of my Lord and Master, he gives me; whatever his servant Nanak says comes true, here and hereafter. Now look at who is speaking. Not a customer.
A servant, a daas, someone whose life is already turned toward the Master. That changes the asking. The line isn't a promise that any wish list gets filled.
It's what trust sounds like between a servant and the one he serves: the asking comes out of the relationship, so it already leans toward what the Master would give.
It's the same turn Dhanasri made at its start: fear brought to the Giver, now asking brought to the Master. So the question isn't only what you'd ask for.
It's who you'd be by the time you asked, and whether you'd trust the answer if it came back different.

how: Sikhs read the Gurus' Dhanasri hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib in order, Mahala by Mahala; Guru Arjan's 'jo maangeh thaakur apune te' is sung in kirtan and recited in times of asking.

games.q: someone tells you, 'the Sikh scripture says ask God for anything and you'll get it, so I asked for a car.' what fits ang 681?
o: the line's spoken by a servant, so the asking comes out of trust, not a wish list.
yes, exactly; the line works for any wish if you ask the right way.
no; Sikh teaching says it's wrong to ever ask God for anything.
games.why: Guru Arjan's 'whatever I ask, he gives' is signed by 'his servant Nanak'. the relationship shapes the asking.

practice: Close your eyes and sit still. Let one honest ask come up, whatever it is, without judging it. Then hold it quietly for the rest of the sit, and notice whether it changes shape the longer you hold it.
